text: Course eight established that a Terraform provider is just a plugin — azurerm and aws can both be declared in the same configuration with no conflict. But that alone doesn't make a module multi-cloud. Declaring both providers doesn't let a resource block conditionally become either one, and the real pattern for writing a module that actually targets more than one cloud is more specific than it sounds.

A resource block's type is fixed the moment you write it — azurerm_virtual_network can never transform into aws_vpc at apply time, no matter what variable you set. So the branching happens one level up, at resource selection, not inside a single resource. You declare both resource blocks in the same module, and put count on each one: count equals var.cloud equals azure, one or zero, and the mirror condition on the AWS side. Whichever branch doesn't match evaluates to zero instances and simply doesn't exist in state.

The payoff shows up in the output block. Regardless of which branch actually ran, the module exposes the same network_id attribute name — pulled from azurerm_virtual_network's id on Azure, or aws_vpc's id on AWS. That's the real portability win: calling code never has to write its own cloud-equals-azure branch, because the module already normalized that difference away before anyone downstream has to think about it.

At any real scale, you don't inline both clouds' resources in one flat file — you nest this same count-per-cloud pattern inside dedicated child modules, and thread var.cloud down from the root exactly once. That keeps the branching contained to one place per concern instead of scattering cloud-equals-azure ternaries through every resource in the configuration, which is what actually keeps a multi-cloud Terraform codebase reviewable instead of a maze.

There's a related but genuinely different pattern worth distinguishing: provider aliasing. If an apply needs to create resources on both clouds at once — replicating data to a second region on a second provider, not choosing between them — you declare a second provider block with an alias and reference it explicitly per resource, with no conditional at all. Next lesson turns to the honest other half of this story: what doesn't port well no matter which pattern you reach for, and when continuing to chase portability actually costs more than it saves.
